Q1.text: Building agents that can effectively create and modify code in complex software systems, while gathering information on the fly to debug problems, is a core unsolved challenge the paper addresses.
Ensuring that agent-driven software development is safe and avoids negative side effects on the user's system is identified as a challenge motivating the work.

Q2.text: The authors consider software the most powerful way humans currently interact with the world, making it the interface they choose for AI agents to act through.
Rapid improvements in LLMs have driven a surge of AI agents able to perceive and act on their environment, motivating a platform to develop and evaluate them.

Q3.text: Prior open-source agent frameworks (e.g. AutoGPT, LangChain, MetaGPT, AutoGen, AutoAgents) each provide interaction interfaces, environments, and communication mechanisms, but the paper argues none combines a standardized tool library, sandboxed code execution, a built-in browser, an agent hub, and an evaluation framework together.

SWE-Agent showed the importance of a carefully crafted agent-computer interface, but the paper notes that creating, maintaining, and distributing such tools across different agent implementations is a difficult engineering challenge.

Q4.text: OpenHands implements an event-stream interaction mechanism connecting user interfaces, agents, and environments through a chronological history of actions and observations.
OpenHands provides a Docker-sandboxed runtime giving agents a bash shell, an interactive Python/Jupyter server, and a Playwright-based Chromium browser.
OpenHands integrates 15 established benchmarks into a single evaluation framework.
OpenHands ships an AgentSkills library of Python utility functions auto-imported into the agent's IPython environment.

Q5.text: The core action set (bash/Python execution, browser interaction) was chosen, inspired by CodeAct, to be a comprehensive yet flexible set of primitives covering most tasks human software engineers and analysts perform.

A new AgentSkill is added only when a capability is not readily achievable by an LLM writing code directly, or when it requires calling an external model, keeping the tool library deliberately minimal.

Q6.text: The evaluation covers 15 benchmarks spanning software engineering, web browsing, and miscellaneous assistance categories.
SWE-Bench Lite evaluation used 300 instances without hint text, for cost-saving reasons.
HumanEvalFix evaluation used the 164-instance Python subset, 0-shot, with multi-turn self-debugging from test feedback.
GPQA evaluation used the 198-instance diamond set as the headline subset, with main and extended subsets reported separately.

Q7.text: CodeActAgent v1.8 with claude-3-5-sonnet resolves 26.0% of SWE-Bench Lite instances.
CodeActAgent fixes 79.3% of HumanEvalFix Python-split bugs in a 0-shot setting.
CodeActAgent v1.8 with claude-3-5-sonnet scores 52.0% on the GPQA diamond set, versus 21.9% for non-expert humans and 81.2-81.3% for expert humans.
CodeActAgent v1.5 with gpt-4o scores 57.6% on AgentBench's OS (bash) subset, versus 42.4% for the AgentBench gpt-4 baseline.

Q8.text: The same CodeAct agent, without modification to its system prompt, performs competitively across software development, web interaction, and miscellaneous-assistance task categories simultaneously.
OpenHands's infrastructure was shown able to integrate and run evaluation across 15 structurally different benchmarks within one framework.

Q9.text: All SWE-Bench results are reported without hint text, so they do not establish performance when hint text is available.
The HumanEvalFix comparison is not apples-to-apples: OpenHands is evaluated 0-shot while the cited SWE-Agent number (87.7%) uses a 1-shot full demonstration trajectory.

Comparisons are restricted to open-source reproducible baselines that do not perform manual prompt engineering specific to the benchmark content, so results do not establish superiority over arbitrarily tuned closed-source or benchmark-tuned baselines.

Q10.text: The primary contribution is a general, open-source, MIT-licensed platform combining an event-stream agent abstraction, a sandboxed Docker runtime, an extensible AgentSkills tool library, multi-agent delegation, and a 15-benchmark evaluation framework.
The contribution includes an AgentHub of over 10 community-contributed agent implementations, led by a CodeAct-based generalist agent.

Q11.text: The authors state that current agents still struggle with complex tasks.
The authors state that current agents suffer significantly when editing long files.
The authors state that OpenHands's workflow still requires substantial handcrafted work, i.e. automatic workflow generation is not yet solved.

Q12.text: OpenHands is a general, MIT-licensed, community-driven platform (not a single fixed agent) for developing and evaluating AI agents that interact with the world through software, with 32K+ GitHub stars and 188+ contributors at time of writing.
Its default CodeAct-based generalist agent performs competitively across software engineering, web browsing, and miscellaneous-assistance benchmarks without per-task prompt tuning.

The current OpenHands/OpenHands GitHub repository has since been repurposed as 'Agent Canvas,' a self-hosted developer control center for coding agents, distinct from the research platform described in the paper; its architecture is now split across separate SDK, client, and automation repositories.
